> I have suggestion for slightly different way to fix this

Changing this at the resolver level would break the invariant of JsonTypeInfo.Type matching the input type. So it would immediately give you InvalidCastException once you attempt to resolve the generic JsonTypeInfo<T> or if you try to deserialize. So this needs to be implemented as an ad hoc resolution mechanism driven by the cache that doesn't change the result when try to look up metadata for non weakly typed serialization scenaria.

> To me this seems like issue in ASP.NET.

Maybe, but it's caused by shipped behavior and APIs that will be hard to fix. At the same time, this solves other SG issues that are not specific to ASP.NET's boxing behavior, like private interface implementation support.

> Fix https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/82457

Seems like the issue shouldn't be closed given that issues raised in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/83631/files#r1142186623 aren't resolved yet.

issue_context.title: Add source gen support for `unspeakable types`
comments:
For contrast, this is how the source generator produces metadata for IAsyncEnumerable's implementations that are visible to the source generator:
```C#
[JsonSerializable(typeof(MyAsyncEnumerable))]
public partial class MyContext : JsonSerializerContext
{
}

public class MyAsyncEnumerable : IAsyncEnumerable<int>
{
    IAsyncEnumerator<int> IAsyncEnumerable<int>.GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
        => throw new NotImplementedException();
}
```
Produces
```C#
jsonTypeInfo = global::System.Text.Json.Serialization.Metadata.JsonMetadataServices.CreateIAsyncEnumerableInfo<global::MyAsyncEnumerable, global::System.Int32>(options, info);
```
It's important to note that we wouldn't be able produce equivalent metadata for private implementations without resorting to `Type.MakeGenericType` calls, which are out of the question for NativeAOT scenaria. This is how the reflection converter factory works today:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/cb8d49aaa4aa4f76e4cee0c2228651e1093188e9/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Converters/Collection/IAsyncEnumerableConverterFactory.cs#L28-L29

One possible solution is that we use [nearest ancestor](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/4cbe6f99d23e04c56a89251d49de1b0f14000427/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Metadata/PolymorphicTypeResolver.cs#L182-L229) resolution logic and fall back to the closest available supertype. This fallback should only happen in [serialization](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/cb8d49aaa4aa4f76e4cee0c2228651e1093188e9/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/Metadata/JsonTypeInfoOfT.WriteHelpers.cs#L278-L285) as generally speaking it could only be supported in contravariant methods. We should never be returning the `JsonTypeInfo` of a supertype in any of the `GetTypeInfo` methods as that would violate the following invariants:
1. `options.GetTypeInfo(type).Type == type` and
2. `options.GetTypeInfo(typeof(T)) is JsonTypeInfo<T>`

We also need to be careful about leaving out fallback to trivial supertypes such as `JsonTypeInfo<object>` as that would always just produce `{}` in JSON.
Why is ASP.NET looking at the runtime type when calling JSON? It should be using return type directly and then the metadata for unspeakable type wouldn't be needed... Am I missing something here?

> Why is ASP.NET looking at the runtime type when calling JSON? It should be using return type directly and then the metadata for unspeakable type wouldn't be needed... Am I missing something here?

Short answer is filters. They can return `object` so any static type information is lost
should they be special casing that on their side then?

They could, although it would be replicating the logic that the PR is introducing. And, as mentioned in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/83631#issuecomment-1476100978 the issue is not specific to boxing, it also addresses the issue of private interface implementation support.

cc @eerhardt

Note, ASP.NET also looks at the runtime type (today) in order to get the intended polymorphism serialization behavior.

See:

* https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/45405
* https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/46008

That should hopefully no longer be needed once https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/77532 is addressed.

> should they be special casing that on their side then?

How would ASP.NET special case it? It only has a single type - the runtime type. There is no "declared type" in filters. The "declared type" is `object`.
And it's not just impacting ASP.NET obviously, we've had our own share of issues filed about this: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/79661
Reopening to track potential changes in the semantics of the feature (enabling via feature flags, etc.)

review_comments: Note that as this exception wasn't thrown, there isn't going to be anything "captured" for it in terms of a stack trace.  Not sure if that matters for your needs.
In this case, I don't think it matters very much.
cc: @GrabYourPitchforks
FWIW this is just falling back to a supported base type for the case of serialization only, so in a way it's the exact opposite of polymorphic serialization.
Are there any situations where this will result in surprising behavior?  Where data will "accidentally" and silently end up being skipped that the developer expected to be serialized?

I expect that there will be, particularly for users moving from reflection to source gen where every input type just works. But I think it's a reasonable trade-off over the current behaviour of simply refusing to handle statically undeclared types.

We debated as to whether the fallback should only apply to "truly inaccessible" types rather than types that could be acciesible by the SG context, but ultimately this would make the fallback more difficult to reason about.

> But I think it's a reasonable trade-off over the current behaviour of simply refusing to handle statically undeclared types.

I'm not convinced of that. Things that would have produced a diagnosable and actionable error are now going to just silently do the "wrong thing" in some cases.

> I'm not convinced of that. Things that would have produced a diagnosable and actionable error are now going to just silently do the "wrong thing" in some cases.

I would say that this fallback creates a loss of fidelity in all cases, not just a few cases. Even in the desirable scenario of, say, a private collection falling back to the contract for `IEnumerable<T>`, we are silently permitting serialization even though the type cannot be roundtripped to its original value (reflection permits that scenario). Still, I think this behaviour is desirable and removes a large hurdle in the adoption of SG, provided of course that we document it thoroughly (i.e. "In SG, serialization has contravariance semantics")

Even in the case of POCOs though, note that the "wrong thing" concerns serializing fewer properties than otherwise contained in the runtime type. STJ does this a in quite a few places already -- we're generally speaking more concerned about the opposite effect, i.e. unconstrained polymorphism serializing more properties than expected. 

I see two possible alternatives:

1. Ship as an opt-in flag in `JsonSerializerOptions` or
2. Restrict to private runtime types falling back to declared interface types, or something along these lines.

For Preview3, I would recommend shipping as-is to give a bit of soak time to the ASP.NET folks and get feedback for the feature in practice.

cc @eerhardt @davidfowl @halter73
Should this be a switch on JsonTypeInfo and a new attribute perhaps? I'd prefer this to be opt-in
or opt-in on options maybe

It doesn't need a flag, the fallback is exploiting the natural contravariance properties of serialization. In other words, it's upcasting your value to a type for which serialization is supported, rather than failing altogether.
aren't there scenarios where user may lose data when using source-gen while it will work just fine for reflection?
could we scope this to only unspeakable types? (i.e. is there something we could use to determine whether that type is unspeakable?)

> aren't there scenarios where user may lose data when using source-gen while it will work just fine for reflection?

Yes. One key difference that holds for every scenario is that unlike reflection you're no longer able to roundtrip the exact value. I think it's an acceptable tradeoff rather than source gen not working at all for the given type.

> could we scope this to only unspeakable types?

Not really. From a reflection perspective you can't determine if a nonpublic type is accessible to the context that's generating metadata. But even if we somehow could tell it's better to have consistent semantics.
Would we need this class if we just attach the nearest ancestor as a prop on `JsonTypeInfo`?

A class is needed because nearest-ancestor resolution is done lazily on the created `CacheEntry`. This is because the algorithm needs to walk the entire hierarchy, necessitating multiple cache lookups that can't be inserted into a single `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd` operation. But because you need to mutate the entry after its insertion, it has to be a class instead of, say, a struct.
You've mentioned private interface implementations a few times in your responses to folks.  Do any of these tests exercise that?
I expect these to be covered by the `IEnumerable` and `IAsyncEnumerable` test inputs.
What properties are implemented explicitly in those cases?  Or maybe I misunderstood what case you were referring to?

If you mean POCO-shaped interfaces, then no, I've skipped that case. The fallback logic is shape-invariant and it's complicated by the fact that interfaces don't support roundtripping OOTB. I'll add a separate test covering that just in case.
nit should this be `private`? It's not called elsewhere.
The class itself is private, but its members are accessed by the containing class.
This approach is clever but worth a comment highlighting how/when the ancestor data is being cached so as to avoid the traversal on every use.
Done.
